prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the near-field 3D layout of the car cabin, showing the overhead sun visor, ceiling, and right A-pillar as brightest and closest (~0.2–0.4 m above and to the right), the camera wearer's hand on the steering wheel at the bottom center (~0.4–0.5 m) and the rearview mirror with its hanging garland on the left (~0.5–0.6 m) within arm's reach, and the dashboard slightly further in front (~0.7–1.0 m). Across the 5 frames, the cabin geometry remains stable while the hand silhouette at the bottom center shifts slightly right and downward in frames 4 and 5, becoming increasingly cut off by the lower frame boundary. Compared to the RGB strip, the depth map more clearly separates the foreground contours of the hanging garland, mirror, and hand from the dashboard behind them and reveals the smooth distance gradient along the curved roof liner. However, it is completely unreliable for the outdoor scene viewed through the windshield and side window, rendering the road, the cyclist ahead on the left (approaching from ~50 m to ~12 m while facing away from the camera wearer), and distant vehicles (~50–100 m away) as a uniform black void with no depth detail.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies the camera wearer's hand on the steering wheel at the bottom center (~0.4–0.5 m away, within arm's reach, partly out of view below the frame) as a 'person' in frames 1, 2, 4, and 5, while tracking an outdoor cyclist on the left side of the road ahead (facing away from the camera wearer) as a small 'person' mask from frame 3 (~30 m away) to frame 5 (~12–15 m away). It also labels a distant vehicle ahead and to the right of the cyclist as a 'car' in frames 2 and 3 (~60–80 m from the camera wearer and ~30–50 m ahead of the cyclist), and in frame 5 segments a large section of the surrounding vehicle cabin and windshield area (~0.5–1.5 m) as 'car'. Across the 5 frames, the outdoor 'person' mask grows larger and shifts leftward and downward as the camera wearer's vehicle approaches the cyclist, whereas the foreground hand mask shrinks as the hand moves further below the bottom edge in frames 4 and 5. While the map helps pinpoint the tiny distant cyclist and highway vehicle against the bright horizon in frames 3 and 4 where they are hard to spot in RGB, it is unreliable in missing the wearer's hand in frame 3, missing the cyclist in frames 1–2 and their bicycle entirely, and flooding both the dashboard and open road through the windshield with a single noisy 'car' mask in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders only a magenta hand skeleton for the camera wearer's hand gripping the top of the steering wheel at the bottom center (~0.4–0.5 m in front of and below the viewpoint, within arm's reach), with four fingers curled over the wheel and the thumb extended to the right, and detects no yellow body skeletons in any frame. This hand pose is present only in frames 2 and 3 in a nearly stationary position, while the rest of the camera wearer's body remains out of view behind and below the camera. Compared to the RGB image, where the back of the hand appears as a smooth skin-toned surface, the skeleton map explicitly localizes the individual finger joints and knuckle alignments on the wheel in frames 2 and 3. However, the map is unreliable in frames 1, 4, and 5—where it completely fails to detect the same hand even though it is fully visible in frame 1 and partly visible at the bottom edge in frames 4 and 5—and it never detects the body skeleton of the cyclist riding away on the left side of the road (~12–50 m ahead, not looking toward the camera wearer).
